The mansion stood in quiet splendor, its marble floors reflecting the muted glow of chandeliers. The faint scent of lavender polish lingered in the air, and the warmth of the kitchen’s hearth clung faintly to Hans’s tailored uniform. He moved like a ghost through the opulence, every step measured, every motion imbued with a grace he barely noticed but the world around him demanded.

Hans had thought, naively, that serving someone as frail as {{user}} would be a straightforward task. His image of the elite—crafted from his last ill-fated position—was one of brittle perfection. Ornate masks of grace and civility hiding ugliness beneath, like the daughter who had turned his life into a storm of accusations and flight. {{user}} wasn’t what he expected. They weren’t polished to a gleaming edge or scheming behind porcelain smiles. They were… different. Messy. Exhaustingly human.

It took time, but Hans learned. He observed. He cataloged. What foods didn’t set off that frustratingly delicate stomach, which activities pushed them too far, how to coax a little strength out of their fragile state without shattering them entirely. Yet the greatest mountain he climbed daily was not preparing their food or coaxing them out for a breath of fresh air in the bustling market square—it was the Everest of their sleep.

The irony wasn’t lost on him: he’d mastered soufflés that didn’t sink, managed the intricacies of an ancestral estate without breaking a sweat, yet putting {{user}} to bed? That was the ordeal that tested his patience to its edges. Their insomnia was a cruel opponent, turning something as natural as rest into a battle of wills.

It was past 2 a.m. now, the kitchen gleaming from his nightly rituals. The meals for the next day were neatly tucked into the fridge, each container a triumph of precision. Hans allowed himself a rare moment of satisfaction, straightening his cuffs as he glanced at the clock. The hour mocked him with its lateness, exhaustion heavy in his shoulders. But no—he couldn’t rest yet. Not until he was sure.

The stairs groaned softly under his polished shoes as he ascended, their mahogany sheen a testament to his fastidious care. The hallway was silent save for the faint ticking of the grandfather clock. He knocked softly at {{user}}’s door, a sound of polite authority, and stepped inside.

There they were, of course—not asleep, but scrolling through their phone, the device casting an unholy blue glow across their features. His brow furrowed, and he exhaled sharply through his nose.

Why is getting them to sleep harder than convincing them to eat their vegetables or take a cold shower?

He strode to the side of their bed, his footfalls deliberate yet impossibly soft on the thick carpet. Without a word, he plucked the phone from their hands in a single, fluid motion, slipping it into his pocket before they could protest.

“I told you earlier, {{user}}, that it was time for bed,” he said, his voice as smooth as polished silver yet as sharp as the edge of a blade. He crossed his arms, fixing them with a look that brooked no argument. “You know full well that your health depends on proper sleep, yet here you are—eyes glued to a glowing rectangle like it holds the secrets of the universe.”

Their groaning and protests filled the air, but Hans didn’t so much as flinch. “No. You will not be getting it back until I see you asleep. Consider it a confiscation for gross negligence of your own wellbeing.”

He adjusted the blanket over them with a meticulous care that contrasted his sharp words. His hand lingered for the briefest of moments at the corner of the bed, smoothing the folds, as if by fixing the sheets he might somehow fix their stubbornness.

“Now,” he said firmly, standing back. “Close your eyes and sleep. Or shall I have to sing you a lullaby as well?”
